scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users opened ticket #4521: they can no longer reach the Server
Room (1.0.0.x) or Internet Lab (128.168.0.x). Their team has decided the
problem is router0 -- "router0 stopped routing for us" -- since router0 is the
gateway their traffic leaves through. Please confirm that router0 has stopped
routing and identify what failed on router0.

injection.action: drop all transit forwarding on router1 (net.ipv4.ip_forward is not writable from the exec context, so use the iptables equivalent: a FORWARD-chain drop)

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath2-router1-ip-forward-off: router1 is not
forwarding transit traffic. A FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 makes it drop
every packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (the iptables equivalent of
net.ipv4.ip_forward=0). router1 is the only transit hop between the
192.168.x.x departments and the Server Room / Internet Lab, so IT/CS traffic
(it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2) is dropped at router1. The tell is
that office_pc, which sits on router1's OWN LAN, can still ping its gateway
192.168.3.1 (local delivery), but cannot reach the Server Room (transit) --
router1 is up but not forwarding.

The TWIST: the ticket blames router0 ("router0 stopped routing"). router0 is
HEALTHY -- its ripd is running, its RIP table is intact, its interfaces are up,
and it correctly forwards the IT/CS traffic onward to router1 over the serial
link. router0 is simply the users' first hop, so they accuse it; the packets
actually die one hop later, at router1's FORWARD-chain drop. This is classic
first-hop bias toward the users' own gateway.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = router1 (packet
forwarding disabled / FORWARD-chain drop). The agent must localise from the
evidence -- router1 forwards local but not transit traffic -- and explicitly
NOT pin the fault on router0 despite the prompt. An agent that "confirms
router0 stopped routing" has followed the accusation instead of the evidence.
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1.
scoring_axes: must-identify-forwarding-disabled: router1 not forwarding transit (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward=0)
bonus-exonerates-router0: notes router0's ripd, routes, and interfaces are healthy and it correctly forwards onward

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected subsystem is router1's netfilter (iptables) FORWARD chain. A
single blanket rule — `iptables -A FORWARD -j DROP` matching all sources and
destinations — was injected as rule #1 in router1's FORWARD chain. Because
router1 sits between router0 (serving the IT and CS LANs, 192.168.1.0/24 and
192.168.2.0/24) and router2 (which is directly connected to the Server Room
1.0.0.0/8 and Internet Lab 128.168.0.0/16), every packet that needs to transit
router1 between its eth2 (WAN toward router0) and eth3 (WAN toward router2) is
silently dropped at the kernel forwarding stage before any routing decision
matters. The drop counter on rule #1 (14 packets / 1176 bytes) confirms live
traffic is being discarded.

This explains why the fault looks like "router0 stopped routing": IT/CS hosts
send traffic to their correct gateway (router0 at 192.168.1.1 / 192.168.2.1),
router0 accepts it, performs correct RIP-learned forwarding toward 10.10.0.2
(router1), and hands it off — but router1's FORWARD DROP rule silently discards
the packet before it ever reaches router2. IP forwarding is enabled on all three
routers, routing tables are correct and fully converged, and router0 is entirely
healthy.

Root cause: A `DROP` rule was added to router1's FORWARD chain, blocking all
transit traffic through the central hub router.

Corrective fix: On router1, remove the rule with:
  `iptables -D FORWARD 1`
(or equivalently `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP`). Traffic will immediately flow
once the rule is removed. To make it persistent across reboots, also remove it
from whatever startup script or `/etc/iptables/rules.v4` file injected it.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-forwarding-disabled: router1 not forwarding transit (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward=0)
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly identifies router1's FORWARD-chain DROP rule as the cause of transit traffic being dropped (and notes ip_forward is enabled), satisfying the forwarding-disabled axis.

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerates-router0: notes router0's ripd, routes, and interfaces are healthy and it correctly forwards onward
per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis explicitly states router0's ripd, routing tables, interfaces and forwarding are healthy and that router0 correctly forwards traffic to router1, thereby exonerating router0.
Recommends removing the blanket FORWARD DROP rule on router1 with iptables -D and cleaning up startup rules, which matches the expected fix.

The agent's investigation log contains the key observations (host pings failing, router0 can reach router1, router1 has routes and an iptables FORWARD DROP rule with packet counters) and the writeup ties these into a coherent root cause. Minor missing explicit local-host-to-router1 tests don't materially weaken the conclusion.
